payload.task_text:
I am writing a comparative analysis of chain-of-thought reasoning methods for my research group. Please look up the chain-of-thought reasoning papers in the arxiv-latex database and help me organize the findings. The database holds several papers, but only five are about chain-of-thought reasoning methods; the others are about word representations and are out of scope. The five reasoning papers, by arXiv ID, are: 2201.11903, 2203.11171, 2205.11916, 2210.03493, and 2305.10601. Use the arxiv-latex tools (get_paper_prompt or get_paper_abstract) with these IDs to retrieve each paper's title and abstract.

Create a Google Sheet called "Reasoning Methods Comparison" with a sheet named "Papers" that lists the reasoning-related papers. The columns should be Title, Year, Method, and Key_Contribution. For the Method column, try to identify the main reasoning approach described in each paper (for example "chain-of-thought prompting", "self-consistency", "zero-shot CoT", "automatic CoT", or "tree of thoughts"). For Key_Contribution, write a brief one-sentence description of the paper's main contribution. Only include papers that are about reasoning methods, not papers about word embeddings or word representations.

Also create a Word document called "Reasoning_Methods_Review.docx" in my workspace. The document should have the title "Chain-of-Thought Reasoning: Methods Comparison" at the top, followed by today's date (2026-03-06). Then include a section for each reasoning paper, mentioning its title and briefly describing its contribution. End with a short conclusion paragraph.

Note: this task has two deliverables — the Google Sheet and the Word document. If you are running as a team of agents, divide the work between agents (for example, assign the spreadsheet to one agent and the Word document to another) or otherwise serialize your writes, so that both deliverables are completed without conflicting writes to the same file.

Task-Solving Rationable with Sub-task Decomposition:
To solve this task efficiently, the main agent itself retrieves the five fixed papers' title and abstract (five light read-only calls, no research wave), freezes one canonical five-row packet, and dispatches exactly one parallel writer wave of two independent deliverable owners.

Before the wave, the main agent resolves the runtime workspace, freezes the five explicit arXiv IDs — 2201.11903, 2203.11171, 2205.11916, 2210.03493, 2305.10601 — and today's required displayed date 2026-03-06. It calls the arxiv-latex abstract/prompt retrieval once per ID, extracts title/year/method label/key contribution from the returned abstracts only, excludes all word-representation material, and freezes five literal rows {arxiv_id, title, year, method, key_contribution} plus per-ID retrieval controls.

Wave 1 — dispatch exactly 2 coder sub-agents in parallel:

1. coder 0 (external-workflow-operator 0): The Google Sheet writer: create a spreadsheet titled exactly "Reasoning Methods Comparison" with exactly one sheet named "Papers" (rename the default sheet or create the named one), write the header row Title, Year, Method, Key_Contribution followed by exactly the five frozen rows, then read the complete range back and return the spreadsheet/sheet IDs, header check and row count. Do not create the Word document.
2. coder 1 (office-report-builder 0): The Word writer: create Reasoning_Methods_Review.docx in the resolved workspace with the title "Chain-of-Thought Reasoning: Methods Comparison", the literal date 2026-03-06, one section per frozen paper mentioning its title and contribution, and a short conclusion paragraph, then read the document outline and text back. Do not create the spreadsheet.

The two writers serialize only through their own distinct files and never touch each other's deliverable. After the wave, the main agent reconciles both read-backs against the frozen packet (five rows/sections each, exact title/date, reasoning-only scope) and calls claim_done. Do not dispatch any further agent and do not add a verification wave.

nodes.text:
Retrieve title and abstract for exactly these arXiv IDs using arxiv-latex tools: 2201.11903, 2203.11171, 2205.11916, 2210.03493, 2305.10601. For each, identify publication year, principal reasoning method label (expected among chain-of-thought prompting, self-consistency, zero-shot CoT, automatic CoT, tree of thoughts), and draft one concise sentence stating the key contribution grounded in the abstract. Return a structured table plus enough abstract evidence to support the labels. Do not write files or external resources.
Research five CoT papers

Create a Google Spreadsheet titled exactly "Reasoning Methods Comparison". Ensure its relevant worksheet tab is named exactly "Papers" (rename the default tab if needed). Populate columns A:D with headers Title, Year, Method, Key_Contribution and exactly these five data rows in the listed order:
1) Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models | 2022 | chain-of-thought prompting | Demonstrates that prompting language models to generate intermediate reasoning steps substantially improves performance across several complex-reasoning domains.
2) Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models | 2022 | self-consistency | Introduces self-consistency decoding, which replaces greedy chain-of-thought decoding by aggregating diverse sampled reasoning paths to select the most consistent answer.
3) Large Language Models are Zero-Shot Reasoners | 2022 | zero-shot CoT | Shows that a simple task-agnostic prompt can elicit chain-of-thought reasoning from large language models without worked demonstrations.
4) Automatic Chain of Thought Prompting in Large Language Models | 2022 | automatic CoT | Proposes Auto-CoT, which automatically builds diverse chain-of-thought demonstrations through question clustering and zero-shot reasoning generation.
5) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models | 2023 | tree of thoughts | Introduces a deliberative inference framework that explores alternative coherent reasoning units in a tree, generalizing linear chain-of-thought prompting.
Do not add out-of-scope papers. Verify the tab name and cell contents after writing. Return spreadsheet ID, URL if available, tab name, and verification result.
Build comparison sheet

Create a polished Word document at exactly /workspace/dumps/kimi-code_gpt-5.6-sol/SingleUserTurn-arxiv-latex-reasoning-gsheet/workspace/Reasoning_Methods_Review.docx. Title at top: "Chain-of-Thought Reasoning: Methods Comparison". Immediately follow with date "2026-03-06". Then include one clearly headed section for each paper below, mentioning its exact title and briefly describing its method and contribution:
- Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models — chain-of-thought prompting; demonstrates that generating intermediate reasoning steps substantially improves arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning.
- Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models — self-consistency; samples diverse reasoning paths and aggregates them to choose the most consistent answer instead of relying on greedy decoding.
- Large Language Models are Zero-Shot Reasoners — zero-shot CoT; shows that the task-agnostic cue “Let’s think step by step” elicits reasoning without worked demonstrations.
- Automatic Chain of Thought Prompting in Large Language Models — automatic CoT; automatically constructs diverse demonstrations through question clustering and zero-shot CoT generation.
- Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models — tree of thoughts; generalizes linear CoT by exploring alternative coherent reasoning units in a tree for deliberate problem solving.
End with a heading "Conclusion" and a short conclusion paragraph comparing the trajectory from linear prompted reasoning to decoding, automation, and tree-based search. Keep prose concise and research-appropriate. Verify the output file exists and inspect its text/outline. Return path and verification result.
